title: 15 Million Died of COVID, and Nobody Ran an Independent Investigation
dek: Gurley lines COVID up next to 737 Max, Hurricane Katrina, Fukushima and the Challenger, and finds an anomaly: every other disaster got an independent investigation and accountability. Six years into COVID, not even the root cause has been investigated.
why: Not an AI topic — it's Bill Gurley's full argument on COVID origins. High information density, but the position is unmistakable; judge it yourself.
who: Founders and investors interested in COVID origins, institutional failure and investigative journalism; anyone who wants to see the non-AI side of Bill Gurley.
skip: The first 18 minutes of disaster case studies — skip straight past 18:08 if you already know them.

points.h: Gurley isn't talking about AI this time — he's talking about something that weighed on him for six years
points.body: He says up front: this is not an AI talk, it's a serious topic, there probably won't be many jokes. He says it has been weighing on him for five or six years, and he hopes spreading it can have an impact. He starts with a run of disasters — the Surfside condo collapse in Florida, the two 737 Max crashes, Hurricane Katrina, Fukushima, the Challenger — and breaks each into two layers, "technical failure" and "institutional failure," before he gets to COVID. This setup takes up the first two-thirds of the talk and is the core structure of his argument: first prove what should happen after a disaster, then point out that after COVID nothing happened.

points.h: After a disaster there is a standard process, and it's called CAPA
points.body: Gurley says the scientific world has a process for analyzing failure called CAPA — corrective and preventive action — with five steps: discover, investigate, confirm root cause, correct, prevent. He stresses that you cannot skip confirming the root cause, because if you don't know what actually happened you don't know what to fix. CAPA is required by FDA law in pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturing, and aerospace has regulations requiring the same process after a failure. He brings this up to establish a standard: every other disaster went through this process. COVID did not.

points.h: Investigators become blockers, and even the ones hired to investigate change sides
points.body: Gurley repeatedly uses the pair "seekers" and "blockers." In Hurricane Katrina, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built the levees, so it naturally became a blocker. What surprised him more: the Corps hired the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) to do an internal investigation and paid a million dollars, but over time the ASCE people moved inside the Corps and became blockers themselves. University of California professor Raymond Seed later wrote a 42-page report listing every instance of ASCE obstructing the investigation; the document is findable online. Gurley uses this case to show that obstruction isn't necessarily malice — it's an institution's instinctive reaction under the spotlight.

points.h: Fukushima's hero was a doctor, not a nuclear physicist
points.body: Japan's parliament asked Kiyoshi Kurokawa to lead the country's first independent civilian investigation. Commission members were required to have no institutional ties to regulators or the power company, and had full authority to pursue anyone. Kurokawa said he had three principles: care about human safety, the investigation must lead to recommendations, and he knew from Three Mile Island and Chernobyl how much this mattered from a global perspective. Gurley points out specifically: Kurokawa was a doctor, not a nuclear physicist, yet he led the commission with extremely high standards and professionalism. The report came out seven months later, and its first sentence was: "The nuclear power plant accident cannot be regarded as a natural disaster. It was entirely man-made, and it could and should have been avoided."

points.h: Feynman dunked an O-ring in ice water on live TV and snapped it
points.body: After the Challenger disaster, Reagan set up the Rogers Commission, mostly made up of "their own people" — Neil Armstrong, astronauts, generals, NASA executives. Someone suggested adding a physicist, so they approached Feynman. They didn't know Feynman was fiercely independent, hungry for the truth, and had no time for pointless diplomacy. Feynman didn't want to do it, said he hated Washington, and only agreed because his wife talked him into it. The moment he agreed he cleared his calendar for the next six months; no other commissioner did that. Before he even got to Washington he started his own investigation, going to NASA facilities and demanding to see people. Armstrong told him "we're just assessing, not investigating," but it was already too late. On live TV he dunked a piece of O-ring-like material into the glass of ice water in front of him, pulled it out and snapped it, demonstrating the failure. The commission sanded all the sharp edges off his report; he called Rogers and asked to have his name removed, but couldn't — Appendix F is his full notes.

points.h: After COVID, not one of the things that should have happened happened
points.body: Gurley lists them off: no dedicated editorial team of more than 30 investigators working COVID, no major media outlet did it; no sustained investigative reporters with editorial backing in the mold of Gates, Schlesinger, Flackerd; no bipartisan Senate or congressional committee like Katrina or 737 Max; no independent investigation like Feynman's or Kurokawa's; no academically funded investigation — NIST and NSF both launched investigations in the other two cases, but NIH did not fund a third-party investigation; and no mass litigation by victims to find out what happened. He says that in other, far smaller cases, well-intentioned people did all of this, and did it purposefully and meaningfully.

points.h: He names five people: they aren't experts, they're blockers
points.body: Gurley names Francis Collins, Anthony Fauci, Peter Daszak (EcoHealth Alliance), Jeremy Farrar (Wellcome Trust, later WHO), and Ralph Baric (University of North Carolina virologist), saying they aren't experts but blockers, behaving exactly the way the FAA, Boeing and NASA did in the other cases. He gives four reasons: first, they are insiders in the virology world, and when the spotlight hits, the instinct is to circle the wagons and protect themselves; second, they ran a disinformation campaign that steered people away from the answers; third, before COVID they were all public supporters of gain-of-function research — Fauci wrote a 2011 Washington Post column saying the benefits outweighed the risks — and Gurley says if you tell the whole world this must be done because the benefits outweigh the risks, you have zero chance of fairly finding out what happened, because thinking every night that what you did caused 15 million deaths is unbearable, and the brain is more likely to trick you into believing it didn't happen; fourth, and most important, they simply weren't looking.

points.h: The DEFUSE proposal: 78% of scientists had never heard of it
points.body: Three years into COVID, the DRASTIC team found this document, called the DEFUSE proposal. Gurley asks on stage who has heard of it; about three hands go up. No major magazine has reported on the DEFUSE proposal. There is a survey of scientists: asked about the origin of COVID, and if they answered "animal transmission," they were then asked whether they had heard of DEFUSE — only 22% said yes, 78% said they had never heard of it. The document is a proposal from EcoHealth Alliance (Peter Daszak's organization) linking a top virologist at Duke University in North Carolina with Shi Zhengli, the "bat woman" in Wuhan, and proposing to insert a furin cleavage site at the S1-S2 junction of a bat coronavirus, because they believed it would make the virus more virulent in animals. Gurley says he took this to an AI and had it do a "clean session" — not looking at anything it had been told before — and asked how it would react to the DEFUSE proposal if it were guiding an investigation into the origin of COVID using CAPA principles. The AI's answer: a direct investigative lead, an extremely critical and important investigative lead, this is primary documentary evidence, the highest level of evidence. Gurley says if this document had been public in January 2020, the conversation at the time would have been completely different.

terms.def: The standard process for analyzing failure: discover, investigate, confirm root cause, correct, prevent — you cannot skip confirming the root cause.
Research that deliberately makes a virus more dangerous to animals or humans. Obama banned it, then it was discussed for being allowed again.
An EcoHealth Alliance proposal suggesting the insertion of a furin cleavage site at the S1-S2 junction of a bat coronavirus.
A structure at the S1-S2 junction of SARS-CoV-2; the DEFUSE proposal suggested inserting it, and it is thought it could enhance virulence.
A loosely affiliated group of scientists sharing information to trace the origins of COVID; they found the DEFUSE proposal.

quotes.text: Six years later, we still don't know. So excuse me if I'm not afraid of what some AI developer's chatbot will do to humanity when you can't even tell me what the thing has already done.
If, if you have to overcome politeness and seek the truth when seven people have died, then how should you behave when 15 million die?

if you told the world that we absolutely must do this because the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, you have zero chance of being impartial in figuring out what happened, because going to bed every night thinking that what you did led to the deaths of 15 million people is unbearable.

irrefutable evidence of a conspiracy to cover up and deny the possibility that this could well have been a laboratory error, orchestrated at the highest levels of the scientific establishment, and by a selfish group of scientists who deliberately misled the public.
You are not a bad person if you seek the truth, you are a good person if you seek the truth.
We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark. The real tragedy in life is when people are afraid of the light.

This is pure evil. This is madness. This is madness. This is pure evil—bringing people together who are just saying, "Hey, is it possible that this came from Wuhan? You actually funded research into enhancing the functions of viruses. Why is this such a difficult question for them?"
